newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs new smoking cessation drug.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs new smoking cessation drug.

text.p: A U.S. federal advisory committee on Thursday recommended that the Food and Drug Administration approve a drug now taken as an anti-depressant for use as an aid for smoking cessation.
If approved, Glaxo Wellcome Plc's bupropion would be the first drug to help people quit smoking that could be taken in pill form, and the first not to contain nicotine.
Company officials said the drug could be taken once or twice a day either alone or in combination with another cessation product, such as the nicotine patch.
FDA approval was recommended by the agency's Drug Abuse Advisory Committee. The agency is not bound to follow the advice of its outside expert panels, but usually accepts it.

Glaxo Wellcome scientist Andrew Johnston said the idea to use the anti-depressant drug for smoking cessation arose when it was found that many depressed patients who smoked often quit smoking when they took the drug.

Johnston said that if bupropion was approved, it would be the first non-nicotine treatment for smoking cessation -- others, such as the patch, use mild doses of nicotine to try wean people off cigarettes.
Glaxo Wellcome officials said the drug had been on the market since 1989 as a single-dose anti-depressant, and since earlier this year as a staged-release anti-depressant.
It is the staged-release version that will be considered by the FDA for smoking cessation.

The anti-depressant version had caused seizures in some depressed patients, but company officials said that it showed no seizures when used in smoking cessation trials, and that the drug's effectiveness outweighed any risks.
